name: Igede
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (0 state the same rule, 2 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Bergman, Richard. 1971. Vowel sandhi and word division in Igede. Journal of West African Languages 8(1):13-25.
catalog_locator: pp.15-16 (sec. 1.1 Phonology: Tones; Syllables and words); scanned PDF, no text, pages read visually
catalog_quote: Igede has a discrete level tone system with four level tones: high /´/, high-mid /¯/, low-mid (unmarked), and low /`/. Each vowel and syllabic nasal occurs with one of these four tones. Over 250 minimal pairs, triplets, quadruplets, and quintuplets have been found, involving 30 per cent of the total vocabulary collected (about 2,000 items). ... Phonemes combine to form syllables and phonological words. The syllable consists of V (vowel), CV (consonant, vowel), or N (syllabic nasal), each of which always occurs with a single tone. The word is equated with the vowel harmony unit.

new_statements.quote: Typologically, vowel reduction has been shown to occur more in unstressed syllables (Sen 2012: 466). However, Igede lacks stress, which eliminates the place of stress in the case reported in this study. [p. 4] ... There are four contrastive tones in Igede, the High <á>, high-mid <ā>, low-mid <ӓ>, and low <à> tones (Hartell 1993: 230). The low-mid tone is left unmarked in this article. [p. 6]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Igede with an empty rule; this source supplies an explicit 'lacks stress' statement plus a four-tone inventory, so it fills in rather than contradicts the record. Medium confidence because the statement is made in passing by a phonologist working on the language, without supporting data.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Igede has no word stress; word prosody is carried by four contrastive tones (high, high-mid, low-mid, low). The stress remark is a passing statement in the discussion of diachronic vowel loss, not a dedicated prosody section, and no evidence for it is given.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources read describe Igede of Benue State, Nigeria (Adeniyi 2026 works from Oju/Obi-area speakers; Hartell 1993 is the SIL/Wycliffe orthography). No dialect-specific stress claim was found. Adeniyi 2026 cites Bergman 1971 (JWAL, 'Vowel sandhi and word division in Igede'), not the 1981 SIL outline listed here.
